paragraphs.source_en: The frequent presence of mouflon in both the paintings and the archaeological record is another important fact which may confirm the Epipalaeolithic age of the Round Head paintings. The Epipalaeolithic layers dating between the 10th and 8th millennium BP present a predominance of mouflon remains, which has been interpreted as an economy based on the selective hunting of mouflon (Corridi 1998; Di Lernia 1997). The strong emphasis on mouflon in hunting can be explained as purely practical, e. g. that its meat was preferred or that it was hunted for its fur or horns. This would be the most obvious explanation if there was not the same predominance of mouflon in the Round Head paintings. Would the prehistoric painters paint these animals just to remember their utilitarian functions?

paragraphs.source_en: This does not seem to be the case, as mouflon are frequently located next to masked or decorated anthropomorphic figures, so that their function seems to be a "spiritual" one (see figure 3-6). According to the paintings, the mouflon is clearly a special and privileged animal, not only because it is, together with the antelope, almost the only species represented, but also because it is represented in scenes definable as "religious".

paragraphs.source_en: If we suppose that the Round Head paintings originated in the Epipalaeolithic age, there is a direct quantitative relationship between the hunted animals and their representation in paintings. However, it would also raise the question as to why the most painted animal, the antelope, is not found so abundantly in the archaeological record. Except at Tin Hanakaten, this quadruped was not significantly represented amongst faunal remains, whereas mouflon remains were found not only in the mountain sites but also in the surrounding lowlands associated with the Epipalaeolithic sites in the open (Cremaschi&Di Lerina 1998).

paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the mouflon remains, a comparable situation occurs in the Iberomaurusian, the Epipalaeolithic culture of the North Africa, dated to between the 22th and 10th millennium BP (Aumassip 1986). In almost all Iberomaurusian sites the mouflon (Ammotragus lervia) largely prevails and it sometimes represents 90% of all faunal remains, which is the same percentage as in the excavated sites of the Acacus. Morel (1978) interprets this predominance as selective hunting but Saxon (1976) interprets it as an attempt at pre-domestication of mouflon.
